archetype.name: Cup Contender (possession juggernaut)
archetype.definition: A team that controls 5-on-5 play as well as almost anyone in the league and has a record to match, held back mainly by goaltending and special teams it can fix.

report.headline: The Devils own the puck; the goaltending and penalty kill are the only drag.
report.take:
New Jersey is 13-5-0 and the record is the least impressive thing about it. The Devils take a 57.3% share of the 5-on-5 expected goals and 57% of the shot attempts, both second in the league. They put 32.4 shots a game on net, also second, and allow 19.9, the fewest anywhere and about seven fewer than the league average of 27. That is a team holding the puck for most of the night, and it is a big step up from last season's 49.5% expected-goals share and from the 56% of the 112-point 2022-23 team.

The engine is Jack Hughes: 25 points, 73 shots and a 63.3% expected-goals share in 20.6 minutes a night, fourth among the league's centers on the site. He has plenty of support. Bratt has 15 assists, Hischier and Gritsyuk have eight goals each, and Luke Hughes logs 24.4 minutes and sits seventh among defensemen. That depth is why the forwards grade A- and the blueline A. The Devils are a top-seven team at both ends by goals a game, and the 66-51 goal count was built across the lineup, not by one line.

The numbers don't flatter them, which is the encouraging part. All-situations shooting is 11.1%, 20th and a touch under the league's 11.6%. Save percentage is .891, exactly league average. PDO is 99.3 at 5-on-5. Pts vs Goal Diff is +1.5, a small edge from close games. The real leaks are elsewhere. The goalies are 5.8 goals below expected, 28th. The penalty kill is 29th at 67.6%, more than nine points under the league. The power play is 24th despite Hughes and Hischier. A team ranked second in shot share is still giving away goals in the two areas where shot share doesn't help.

The recent run needs a caveat. Nine wins in ten and five straight is real form, but three of the last four wins came in overtime, each by a goal. The 5-1 at Dallas and 4-0 at Toronto are the truer signal. The 118-point pace will cool, but the floor here is high, and the ceiling rises if the crease and the kill catch up to the 5-on-5 game.

strengths.title: Best shot suppression in the league
strengths.body: New Jersey allows 19.9 shots a game, first in the league and far below the league's 27. It also wins the expected-goals share at a second-best 57.3%. This comes from structure and puck possession, not hot goaltending, so it is the most durable part of the profile. Even a mediocre goalie wins a lot behind numbers like these.

strengths.title: Jack Hughes and real depth
strengths.body: Hughes is driving play at an elite level: 25 points with a 63.3% expected-goals share. Behind him, Bratt, Hischier, Gritsyuk and Evangelista all post on-ice expected-goals shares above 60%, which is why the forwards grade A-. Luke Hughes, Pesce and Hamilton give the blueline an A. Depth like that holds up when one piece cools off.

strengths.title: Scoring without lucky finishing
strengths.body: The Devils score 3.67 a game, seventh in the league, while shooting a below-average 11.1%. Volume is doing the work, with 32.4 shots a game. Timo Meier has three goals on 70 shots, and that kind of drought tends to correct. There is more scoring to come, not less.

concerns.title: Goaltending below expected
concerns.body: The goalies are 5.8 goals below expected, 28th in the league. Nearly all of it belongs to Jake Allen: a .881 save percentage and -5.2 GSAx in nine starts. Connor Hellebuyck has a .913 save percentage, 0.8 GSAx and a shutout in five starts. Who gets the net matters more than anything else on this roster.

concerns.title: A bottom-four penalty kill
concerns.body: A 67.6% kill ranks 29th, 9.4 points under the league average. That is jarring for a team this stingy at 5-on-5. Shorthanded goaltending is likely part of it, which ties back to the crease. The four straight seasons of 79-83% kills in the history suggest this rebounds, but for now it gives back what even strength earns.

concerns.title: Power play and defensemen leaks
concerns.body: The power play converts 19.3%, 24th, with Hughes, Hischier and Bratt all on it. Opponents' defensemen also produce more against New Jersey than their averages predict, 25th in the league. That makes sense for a team that concedes the perimeter while protecting the slot, so it is a quirk more than a flaw.

trend.note: A 9-5 October, with 3.43 goals for a game, became a 4-0 November, with 4.5. The last ten went 9-1-0 with a goal differential of 1.7 a game, although three of the four November wins needed overtime.

weekAhead.headline: A weak Winnipeg, then a home-and-home against Washington
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Winnipeg against a Jets team that is 7-8-3 and 27th on the site. Winnipeg allows 33.2 shots a game, the most in the league, and saves at .881, 26th. That is an ideal opponent for a team that leads the league in shot suppression and is second in shot volume. Anything short of controlling that game would be a surprise.

Washington is the real test, twice in three nights. The Capitals are 9-6-0 with a 54% expected-goals share, fifth, and shoot 12.7%, seventh, so they can finish chances. But they are 22nd in goals against, and their wingers give up the third-most points relative to expectation. Their 76.5% kill is around league average, which leaves room for the Devils' power play to get going.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against Winnipeg's leaky net
keyMatchups.body: The Jets allow the most shots in the league and save .881. New Jersey's second-ranked shot volume should produce plenty of goals even at its modest finishing rate.

keyMatchups.title: Bratt and Gritsyuk against Washington's wings
keyMatchups.body: Washington ranks 28th in holding wingers under their averages. That suits Bratt, with 15 assists, and Gritsyuk, with eight goals. The Devils' wings should get chances in both games.

keyMatchups.title: Capitals' finishing against NJ goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Washington shoots 12.7% and is eighth in scoring, so it is the one opponent this week able to punish soft goaltending. Which goalie starts these games matters.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net against Washington, and whether the penalty kill holds against a team that finishes its chances.

restOfSeason.body:
The 5-on-5 dominance is the sustainable part. A team second in expected-goals share and first in shots against, with average save percentage and below-average shooting, is not living on luck. What won't last is the run of one-goal overtime wins and the 118-point pace. Expect the Devils to stay near the top of the Metropolitan with Carolina, which is 14-3-2.

The upside is in the leaks, which point toward improvement. Meier's finishing should come back, the penalty kill has history on its side, and a larger share of starts for Hellebuyck would close much of the goaltending gap. If all three move even partway, this is a genuine Cup contender. If Allen keeps getting the bulk of starts at a .881 save percentage, it is still a comfortable playoff team.
swingFactors: How the starts split between Hellebuyck and Allen
Penalty kill recovering toward league average

confidence.note: An 18-game sample, but the shot and expected-goals numbers are strong and settle quickly.
